# Deciphering the preeclampsia-specific immune microenvironment and the role of pro-inflammatory macrophages at the maternal–fetal interface ## Authors - Haiyi Fei1 ([ORCID: 0009-0002-3344-070X](https://orcid.org/0009-0002-3344-070X)) - Xiaowen Lu1 - Zhan Shi1 - Xiu Liu1 - Cuiyu Yang1 - Xiaohong Zhu4 - Yuhan Lin1 - Ziqun Jiang1 - Jianmin Wang1 - Dong Huang1 - Liu Liu1 - Songying Zhang1 ([ORCID: 0000-0001-8044-6237](https://orcid.org/0000-0001-8044-6237)) † - Lingling Jiang1 ([ORCID: 0000-0002-3343-6279](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-3343-6279)) † ### Affiliations 1. Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, Zhejiang Xiaoshan Hospital Hangzhou China ([ROR:02kzr5g33](https://ror.org/02kzr5g33)) † Corresponding author ## Abstract Preeclampsia (PE), a major cause of maternal and perinatal mortality with highly heterogeneous causes and symptoms, is usually complicated by gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM). However, a comprehensive understanding of the immune microenvironment in the placenta of PE and the differences between PE and GDM is still lacking. In this study, cytometry by time of flight indicated that the frequencies of memory-like Th17 cells (CD45RA−CCR7+IL-17A+CD4+), memory-like CD8+ T cells (CD38+CXCR3−CCR7+Helios−CD127−CD8+) and pro-inflam Macs (CD206−CD163−CD38midCD107alowCD86midHLA-DRmidCD14+) were increased, while the frequencies of anti-inflam Macs (CD206+CD163−CD86midCD33+HLA-DR+CD14+) and granulocyte myeloid-derived suppressor cells (gMDSCs, CD11b+CD15hiHLA-DRlow) were decreased in the placenta of PE compared with that of normal pregnancy (NP), but not in that of GDM or GDM&PE. The pro-inflam Macs were positively correlated with memory-like Th17 cells and memory-like CD8+ T cells but negatively correlated with gMDSCs. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed that transferring the F4/80+CD206− pro-inflam Macs with a Folr2+Ccl7+Ccl8+C1qa+C1qb+C1qc+ phenotype from the uterus of PE mice to normal pregnant mice induced the production of memory-like IL-17a+Rora+Il1r1+TNF+Cxcr6+S100a4+CD44+ Th17 cells via IGF1–IGF1R, which contributed to the development and recurrence of PE. Pro-inflam Macs also induced the production of memory-like CD8+ T cells but inhibited the production of Ly6g+S100a8+S100a9+Retnlg+Wfdc21+ gMDSCs at the maternal–fetal interface, leading to PE-like symptoms in mice. In conclusion, this study revealed the PE-specific immune cell network, which was regulated by pro-inflam Macs, providing new ideas about the pathogenesis of PE. ## Introduction In recent years, low fertility is a global problem (Agbaglo et al., 2022), exacerbated by pregnancy complications. Preeclampsia (PE) is a progressive systemic disease during pregnancy, with pregnancy-induced hypertension, proteinuria, and liver and kidney injury as the main diagnostic indicators (Chappell et al., 2021). With a global prevalence of 7–10%, PE is a major cause of maternal and perinatal mortality and morbidity, especially in low- and middle-income countries. The only specific treatment is delivery (Chappell et al., 2021). However, due to the variety of symptoms and the heterogeneity of the disease, the pathogenesis of PE is still unclear (Burton et al., 2019; Grotegut, 2016). PE is often complicated by gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), which is characterized by insulin resistance and associated with aberrant maternal immune cell adaption (Corrêa-Silva et al., 2018; McElwain et al., 2021; McIntyre et al., 2019). Studies have shown that GDM is an independent risk factor for PE (Nerenberg et al., 2013; Ostlund et al., 2004; Schneider et al., 2012). However, whether a different pathogenesis underlies between PE and GDM is still unclear. The fetus is equivalent to a semi-homogenous graft for the mother. Therefore, maternal–fetal immune tolerance plays an important role in the maintenance of pregnancy. Currently, the pivotal mechanism underpinning the pathogenesis of PE is widely acknowledged to involve an increased frequency of pro-inflammatory M1-like maternal macrophages (Faas et al., 2014; Yao et al., 2019), along with an elevation in granulocytes that capable of superoxide generation (Lampé et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2021), CD56+ CD94+ natural killer (NK) cells (Bachmayer et al., 2006; Travis et al., 2020), CD19+CD5+ B1 lymphocytes (Jensen et al., 2012; LaMarca et al., 2011; Zhong et al., 2007), and activated γδ T cells (Chatterjee et al., 2017). Conversely, this pathological process is accompanied by a notable decrease in the frequency of anti-inflammatory M2-like macrophages (Faas et al., 2014; Yao et al., 2019) and NKp46+ NK cells (Fukui et al., 2011). Adaptive immune response is also critical for the pathogenesis of PE (Deer et al., 2023). In PE, CD4+ T cells prefer to differentiate into pro-inflammatory Th1 and Th17 (Eghbal-Fard et al., 2019; Fu et al., 2014; Lang et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2020; Saito et al., 2007) instead of non-inflammatory Th2 and Treg (Care et al., 2018; Cornelius et al., 2015a; Saito et al., 2007; Santner-Nanan et al., 2009; Sasaki et al., 2007). Moreover, PE can be subdivided into early- and late-onset PE diagnosed before 34 weeks or from 34 weeks of gestation, respectively. Research has revealed that among the myriad of cellular alterations in PE, pro-inflammatory M1-like macrophages and intrauterine B1 cells display an augmented presence at the maternal–fetal interface of both early- and late-onset PE patients. Decidual natural killer cells and neutrophils emerge as paramount contributors, playing a more crucial role in the pathogenesis of early-onset PE (Aneman et al., 2020). However, a comprehensive and in-depth understanding of the maternal–fetal interface of PE is still lacking. The immune cells crosstalk with each other at the maternal–fetal interface elaborately. For example, the interaction between B2 and Th cells depends on CD40 and its ligand CD40L, which helps B2 cells provide AT1-AAs and differentiate into memory B cells in reducing uterine perfusion pressure (RUPP) rats (Cornelius et al., 2015b). The cytokines derived from NK cells can promote the differentiation of Th17 to co-work in recurrent miscarriage (Fu et al., 2013). The intricate interplay and precise coordination between immune cells are pivotal in maintaining pregnancy. Nevertheless, the regulation of the immune network at the maternal–fetal interface of PE patients still needs to be further studied. In this study, we combined cytometry by time of flight (CyTOF), single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), and rodent experiment to identify the overall immune cell composition and their interactions at the maternal–fetal interface in PE, GDM, and GDM complicated with PE (GDM&PE). This study revealed the PE-specific immune cell network, which was regulated by pro-inflammatory macrophages, providing new ideas about the pathogenesis of PE. ## Results ### Overall immune cell profile in the placenta of PE, GDM, and GDM&PE To fully characterize the immune microenvironment at the maternal–fetal interface of PE, we collected full-term placentas of PE and NP, and did a CyTOF test (Table 1), which panel is shown in Table 2. Since PE is usually complicated by GDM, the subjects of GDM and GDM complicated with PE (GDM&PE) were also included. The experimental workflow for CyTOF is shown in the schematic diagram (Figure 1A). We found that in addition to the well-known macrophages and T cells, there are also γδ T cells, B cells, NK cells, granulocytes, dendritic cells, and myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs). An overall distribution of CD45+ cell subsets in placenta as shown in the t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) maps (Figure 1B). There were no significant differences in the proportion of these large subpopulations comparing the PE, GDM, GDM&PE group to the NP group (Figure 1C). To identify the 10 cell subpopulations, CD4, CD8, and γδTCR were used as markers to distinguish CD4+ T, CD8+ T, and γδ T cells. CD11b is a marker that distinguishes myeloid cells, including macrophages and granulocytes (Figure 1D). The 10 cell subsets were further annotated by 41 markers in the heatmap (Figure 1E, Table 3). **Table 1.** Details of the individuals included in the cytometry by time of flight (CyTOF).

### Specific altered T cell profile in the placenta of PE To gain a comprehensive understanding of the distribution patterns within each cellular subset, we conducted separate clustering analyses for CD4+ T, CD8+ T, and γδ T cells, respectively. We first analyzed 15 clusters of CD4+ T cells from the placentas of NP, PE, GDM, and GDM&PE (Figure 2A). CD4+ T cell clusters were defined by canonical marker set signatures (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A). The frequencies of memory-like CD45RA−CCR7+CD69−CD127lowTIGIT−Helios−CD4+ T ells (cluster 8) were significantly increased in individuals with PE compared with NP controls. At the same time, there was no significance in the GDM and GDM&PE groups compared with the NP group (Figure 2B, Table 4). We analyzed the expression of common intracellular molecules in CD4+ memory-like T cells by sorting CD45RO+CCR7+CD4+ T cells from placental samples by flow cytometry. Higher levels of IL-17A and lower levels of Foxp3 were found in memory-like CD45RO+CCR7+CD4+ T cells in the placentas of individuals with PE (Figure 2C). Consistent with the results of CyTOF, higher fluorescence intensity of CD45RO+CD4+ T cells was found in the placentas of individuals with PE than that of NP, and this cell population was mainly located in the placental sinusoids (Figure 2D), suggesting that these T cells should be recently recruited. Moreover, lower expression of immune checkpoint molecules including T-cell immunoglobulin mucin-3 (Tim-3) and programmed cell death 1 (PD-1) was found in CD45RA−CCR7+CD4+ memory T cells in the PE group, suggesting that these cells have a lower immunosuppressive capacity (Chen et al., 2022b; Fanelli et al., 2021; Rasmussen et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2016), there was no significant difference in the GDM or GDM&PE groups comparing with the NP group (Figure 2E). Then, 18 clusters of CD8+ T cells were analyzed (Figure 2F). CD8+ T cell clusters annotation was based on the expression of canonical marker signatures (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B). CD38+CXCR3−CCR7+Helios−CD127− (cluster 2) memory-like CD8+ T cells were significantly increased in the PE group (Figure 2G, Table 4). CD38+CXCR3−CCR7+Helios−CD127− memory-like CD8+ T cells of the PE group expressed lower levels of PD-1 and TIGIT, suggesting the activation of cytotoxicity of these cells (Figure 2H; Morita et al., 2020). Then, 22 clusters of γδT cells were analyzed and annotated (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D). Cluster 15 (HeliosmidCD28midCD69midHLA-DRmidCD127midγδT cells), with lower expression of Tim3, was significantly decreased in the PE group (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, F). In conclusion, significant changes in placental T cell profile were found in the placentas of PE but not in those of GDM or GDM&PE, suggesting that abnormal activation of T cells in the placenta is associated with the pathogenesis of PE. ### Abnormal polarization of macrophages was correlated with specific immune cell subsets in individuals with PE Except for T cells, we also analyzed 29 clusters of CD45+CD3−CD11b+ cells from placentas of NP, PE, GDM, and GDM&PE, including 9 clusters of macrophages, 11 clusters of granulocytes, and 5 clusters of NK/NK-like cells (Figure 3A). The clusters of CD45+CD3−CD11b+ cells were defined by canonical marker set signatures (Figure 3B). Moreover, significantly decreased frequencies of CD68midCD39midHLA-DRlowCD11b+CD15+ granulocytes (cluster 12), which are identified as gMDSCs, were found in the PE group (Figure 3C, Table 4). In addition, the frequency of anti-inflammatory macrophages (anti-inflam Macs) (CD206+CD163−CD86midCD33+HLA-DR+, cluster 25) was also significantly decreased, whereas the frequency of pro-inflammatory macrophages (pro-inflam Macs) (CD206−CD163−CD38midCD107alowCD86midHLA-DRmidCD14+, cluster 23) was significantly increased in the PE group (Figure 3C, Table 4). However, the frequencies of macrophages and gMDSCs were unchanged significantly in the GDM or GDM&PE groups. ![Figure 3.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/100002/elife-100002-fig3-v1.jpg) **Figure 3.:** (A) Distribution of the CD11b+ immune cells in group analyzed using t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE). Data were compared between NP and PE, NP and GDM, and NP and GDM&PE using the Kruskal–Wallis test and represented as mean ± SEM (*p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001; NS, not significant). Pearson correlation analysis indicated positive correlations between pro-inflam Macs (cluster 23 in CD11b+ cells) and CD4+ memory-like T cells (cluster 8 of CD4+ T cells), as well as CD8+ memory-like T cells (cluster 2 in CD8+ T cells). CD206− pro-inflam Macs were negatively correlated with gMDSCs (cluster 12 in CD11b+ cells), but were not statistically significant. Conversely, CD206+ anti-inflam Macs (cluster 25 in CD11b+ cells) were positively correlated with gMDSCs and negatively correlated with CD8+ memory-like T cells (Figure 3D, E). These results suggested that abnormally polarized CD206− pro-inflam Macs are positively correlated with memory-like CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in the placentas of individuals with PE and negatively correlated with gMDSCs. ### F4/80+CD206− pro-inflam Macs induced immune imbalance at the maternal–fetal interface and PE-like symptoms Though increased pro-inflam Macs have been reported in the placenta from individuals with PE (Faas et al., 2014), few studies have reported the interaction between macrophages and other immune cells in the placenta. In this study, transcriptome RNA-seq was used to analyze the difference between CD45+F4/80+CD206− pro-inflam Macs and CD45+F4/80+CD206+ anti-inflam Mac isolated from the uterus and placentas of mice with reducing uterine perfusion pressure (RUPP) (Figure 4A). The diagrammatic representation of the RUPP model is presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A. To establish the PE mouse model, we ligated uterine arteries in pregnant mice on day 12.5 of gestation, and mice with sham operation were considered as controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A). We found that mice of RUPP showed an increased embryo absorption rate, decreased fetal weight, and pup crown-rump length compared with the sham operation group (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B). Increased systolic blood pressure (SBP) and urine albumin creatine ratio (UACR) were also observed in mice with RUPP, which indicated a successful PE mice mode was built (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C). Then, we injected the PE mice derived macrophages into normal pregnant mice. An increased embryo resorption rate, decreased fetal top-rump length and fetal weight were found in mice injected with PE mice derived macrophages compared with mice injected PBS (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D). These data suggested that pro-inflam Macs could induce the production of memory-like Th17 via the IGF1–IGF1R, leading to the development of PE. ## Discussion PE, a progressive systemic disease during pregnancy, is closely related to the alterations in the immune environment at the maternal–fetal interface. In this study, the overall immune cell profiles in the placenta of individuals with NP, PE, GDM, and GDM&PE were detected by CyTOF and a PE-specific change in immune microenvironment of maternal–fetal interface was described for the first time. Further, we provided a novel insight that pro-inflam Macs induced memory-like Th17 cells, memory-like CD8+ T cells, and suppressed the production of gMDSCs in mice maternal–fetal interface by scRNA-seq. In addition, we first validated that IGF1–IGF1R was involved in producing memory-like Th17 cells induced by pro-inflam Macs in vitro and in vivo, thus leading to the development of PE. Various studies represented the effect of a single subset of immune cells in the pathogenesis of PE or GDM (Bachmayer et al., 2006; Care et al., 2018; Cornelius et al., 2015a; Eghbal-Fard et al., 2019; Faas et al., 2014; Fu et al., 2014; Fukui et al., 2011; Lampé et al., 2015; Lampé et al., 2011; Lang et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2020; Santner-Nanan et al., 2009; Sasaki et al., 2007; Travis et al., 2020; Yao et al., 2019). Miller et al., 2022 provided an overall analysis of immune cells in the human placental villi in the presence and absence of spontaneous labor at term by scRNA-seq (Miller et al., 2022). Luo et al. unveiled the intricate interplay existing between SPP1+M1 cells and the IGFBP1+SPP1+ extracellular villous trophoblast in the context of PE by using scRNA-seq (Luo et al., 2023). Li et al. highlighted a key role of a distinct perivascular inflammatory CD11chigh decidual macrophages subpopulation in the pathogenesis of PE through scRNA sequencing (Li et al., 2024). However, the immune cells crosstalk with each other at the maternal–fetal interface elaborately. A comprehensive and in-depth understanding of the immune microenvironment at the maternal–fetal interface of PE is still lacking. Here, we used CyTOF and scRNA-seq to comprehensively analyze the immune cell profile and explore the interaction of immune cells in PE. Additionally, most previous studies have reported immune cells from maternal systemic circulation rather than directly from the tissue of maternal–fetal interface (Cornelius et al., 2015b; Deer et al., 2021; Santner-Nanan et al., 2009; Shields et al., 2018; Wallace et al., 2012). In this study, cells were directly isolated from the tissue of maternal–fetal interface, which is considered as a more accurate approach to unveil the real immune environment of the maternal–fetal interface. Abnormal inflammatory responses were reported to play an important role in the pathogenesis of both PE and GDM (Aneman et al., 2020; Corrêa-Silva et al., 2018; Deer et al., 2023; Jung et al., 2022; McElwain et al., 2021). However, it is unclear how the maternal–fetal interface immune microenvironment differs between the two diseases. We analyzed the overall placental immune cell profile in NP, PE, GDM, and GDM&PE by CyTOF and revealed a PE-specific immune cell profile: The frequencies of memory-like Th17 cells (CD45RA−CCR7+IL-17A+CD4+), memory-like CD8+ T cells (CD45RA−CCR7+CD38+pAKTmidCD127lowCD8+) and pro-inflam Macs (CD206−CD163−CD38midCD107alowCD86midHLA-DRmidCD14+) were increased, while the decreased frequencies of CD69hiHeliosmidCD127mid γδT cells, anti-inflam Macs (CD206+CD163−CD86midCD33+HLA-DR+CD14+) and gMDSCs (CD11b+CD15hiHLA-DRlow) were observed in the placenta of PE, but not in that of GDM or GDM&PE compared with that of NP. PE is often divided into two subtypes based on the time of onset. Late-onset PE, occurring at 34 weeks of gestation or later, accounts for most PE cases, while early-onset PE, occurring before or at 33 weeks of gestation (Lisonkova and Joseph, 2013). However, our previous study observed no significant difference in the M1/M2 macrophage polarization in placentas with early- or late-onset PE (Liu et al., 2022). Therefore, our research was conducted regardless of the PE-onset type to ensure consistency in macrophage polarization of the two subtypes. There have been studies indicating that pro-inflammatory macrophages, Th17 and CD8+ T cells play an essential role in PE development (Care et al., 2018; Eghbal-Fard et al., 2019; Lager et al., 2020; Yao et al., 2019). Macrophages was indicated with a pro-inflammatory phenotype in the placenta with PE (Faas et al., 2014; Yao et al., 2019). Care et al., 2018 reported that placental Tregs helped suppress inflammation at the maternal–fetal interface. Similarly, Lu et al., 2020 found an abnormal increase of IL-17A in the placenta in the development of PE. Meanwhile, the abnormal infiltration of CD8+ T cells in the placenta may contribute to PE (Lager et al., 2020). Consistent with the previous findings, we found that memory-like CD4+ and memory-like CD8+ T cells significantly increased in the PE group and that IL-17A was significantly higher expressed in CD4+ memory-like T cells from the PE group, which is vital in vascular inflammation, leading to the development of PE (Amador et al., 2014; Madhur et al., 2021). Though memory T cells play a key role in fetal–maternal tolerance in NP (Kieffer et al., 2019), few studies have reported the characteristics of memory-like T cells in the development of PE. We constructed an adoptive transferred mouse model. The injection of CD4+ T cells from RUPP mouse, characterized by an increased frequency of Th17 cells and a reduced frequency of Tregs, induced PE-like symptoms in pregnant mice. Tregs which are well known to undergird maternal tolerance of the fetus, and which are well known to have an overlapping developmental trajectory with RORgt+ Th17 cells (Robertson et al., 2019; Sefik et al., 2015). This study underscores the importance of Th17/Treg cell balance in maintaining pregnancy homeostasis. And it is worth noting that we isolated CD4+ memory-like T cells directly from the maternal–fetal interface, which is different from previous studies that the CD4+ T cells for adoptive transfer were isolated from the spleen and induced in vitro (Cornelius et al., 2015b; Deer et al., 2021; Shields et al., 2018; Wallace et al., 2012). Recurrence is an important concern in individuals with PE (Bernardes et al., 2019). We found that a prior PE pregnancy increased the probability of PE in the next pregnancy in mice, accompanied by an increased frequency of memory-like Th17 cells at the maternal–fetal interface, suggesting that increased memory-like Th17 cells are positively related to the recurrence of PE. However, further studies are needed to confirm the function of the fetal-specific memory Th17 cells in the recurrence of PE. Activation of CD8+ T and Th1 cells can be induced by abnormal polarized macrophages in recurrent miscarriage (Li et al., 2022a). The gMDSCs have been reported to have immune suppressive activity and are necessary for maintaining maternal–fetal tolerance (Köstlin-Gille et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2018). However, the correlation between macrophages and other immune cells in the development of PE remained unclear. We verified that pro-inflam Macs induced memory-like Th17 cells and memory-like CD8+ T cells and inhibited the production of gMDSCs in PE by correlation analysis and adoptive transfer in animal experiments for the first time, indicating that the immune cells orchestrate a network in the maternal–fetal interface elaborately. However, PLX3397, used in this study, emerges as a promising small-molecule compound, endowed with the capability to traverse the placental barrier, thereby potentially influencing the development and function of fetal macrophages. In addition to gMDSCs, we conducted immunofluorescence analysis of placental tissue, specifically targeting CD66bhigh neutrophils. Our findings revealed a pronounced increase in the proportion of neutrophils among PE patients, fostering the hypothesis that IL-17A produced by Th17 cells might orchestrate the migration of neutrophils toward the placental milieu. This migratory response, in turn, could potentially trigger reactive oxygen species-mediated immunopathology, which subsequently lead to PE (Akkari et al., 2024). The function of IGR1 and IGF1R in PE is controversial. IGF1 plays a significant role in maintaining immune function, and IGF1R facilitates the differentiation of naive CD4+ T into Th17 cells (DiToro et al., 2020). A study showed that IGF1R was downregulated in the serum of individuals with PE (Liao et al., 2021). Decreased amounts of IGF1R were also found in the placentas of individuals with PE (Robajac et al., 2015). However, another study found no significance in the affinity and the number of IGF1R between placentas from individuals with PE or not (Díaz et al., 2005). We found that mice exhibiting PE symptoms had significantly enhanced IGF1–IGF1R interaction between inflammatory macrophages and memory-like Th17 cells by analyzing the data of scRNA-seq. Then, this finding was further confirmed in human placentas from individuals with PE and NP, for the frequencies of IGF1+ CD14+ and IGF1R+ CD4+ cells were found to significantly increase in the PE group. In vitro, we found that PE-EV-treated macrophages secreted more IGF1 than NP-EV-treated macrophages and induced a higher frequency of memory-like Th17 cells. The inhibition of IGF1R on CD4+ naive T cells resulted in a decreased frequency of memory-like Th17 cells, implying that the IGF1–IGF1R is critical for the production of memory-like Th17 cells induced by inflammatory macrophages. Animal experiments confirmed that IGF1R inhibition on CD4+ T cells at the maternal–fetal interface reduced the frequency of memory-like Th17 cells and relieved PE-like symptoms. In addition, placentas from different groups for CyTOF analysis and flow cytometry were matched by age, preterm pregnancies, and previous abortion history; however, there are differences in body mass index, gestational age, term pregnancies, and the number of living children. Obesity can increase inflammatory and oxidative stress markers in the placental environment (Spradley et al., 2015). Also, it has been reported that the placental immune state shifts with gestational age (Lewis et al., 2018). However, as PE is often accompanied by obesity and early termination of pregnancy, it is difficult to exclude these factors in sample collection. Moreover, limited placental samples in the GDM&PE group are the shortage of this study, for it is hard to collect enough clean samples that exclude interference factors because the number of pregnant women exposed to COVID-19 has increased sharply since December 2022 in China. In summary, this study demonstrated the statistically distinguished placental immune microenvironment in individuals with PE, but not in those with GDM or GDM&PE. More importantly, macrophages orchestrate a network in the maternal–fetal interface elaborately. These findings provide novel insights into PE pathogenesis and a potential immune target for the clinical prevention and treatment of PE. ## Materials and methods ### Clinical sample collection The samples used in this study were collected from Sir Run Run Shaw Hospital between October 2020 and August 2023. ## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.100002.3.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.100002.3.sa1)

Summary:

This study explores the immune microenvironment of the placenta in preeclampsia (PE), which is often accompanied by gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM). Using CyTOF, they found that placentas from PE cases showed increased frequencies of memory-like Th17 cells, memory-like CD8⁺ T cells, and pro-inflammatory macrophages, alongside decreased levels of anti-inflammatory macrophages and granulocyte myeloid-derived suppressor cells (gMDSCs) compared to normal pregnancies. Further analysis revealed a positive correlation between pro-inflammatory macrophages and the expanded T cell populations, and a negative correlation with gMDSCs. Single-cell RNA sequencing provided mechanistic insights: transferring a specific subset of pro-inflammatory macrophages (F4/80⁺CD206⁻ with a distinct gene expression profile) from the uterus of PE mice to normal pregnant mice induced the formation of pathogenic memory-like Th17 cells via the IGF1-IGF1R pathway. This cellular interplay not only contributed to the development but also to the recurrence of PE. Additionally, these macrophages promoted the production of memory-like CD8⁺ T cells while inhibiting gMDSCs at the maternal-fetal interface, culminating in PE-like symptoms in mice. In conclusion, the study identifies a PE-specific immune cell network regulated by pro-inflammatory macrophages, offering new insights into the pathogenesis of preeclampsia.

Strengths:

Utilization of both human placental samples and multiple mouse models to explore the mechanisms linking inflammatory macrophages and T cells to preeclampsia (PE).

Incorporation of cutting-edge and complementary techniques such as CyTOF, scRNA-seq, bulk RNA-seq, and flow cytometry.

Identification of specific immune cell populations and their roles in PE.

Demonstration of the adverse effects of pro-inflammatory macrophages and T cells on pregnancy outcomes through in vivo manipulations.

Comments on revised version:

Several weaknesses were addressed during revision by conducting additional experiments, clarifying the manuscript's text, and incorporating new data that was not initially included.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.100002.3.sa2](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.100002.3.sa2)

Summary:

Fei, Lu, Shi, et al. present a thorough evaluation of the immune cell landscape in pre-eclamptic human placentas by single-cell multi-omics methodologies compared to normal control placentas. Based on their findings of elevated frequencies of inflammatory macrophages and memory-like Th17 cells, they employ adoptive cell transfer mouse models to interrogate the coordination and function of these cell types in pre-eclampsia immunopathology. They demonstrate the putative role of the IGF1-IGF1R axis as the key pathway by which inflammatory macrophages in the placenta skew CD4+ T cells towards an inflammatory IL-17A-secreting phenotype that may drive tissue damage, vascular dysfunction, and elevated blood pressure in pre-eclampsia, leaving researchers with potential translational opportunities to pursue this pathway in this indication.

They present a major advance to the field in their profiling of human placental immune cells from pre-eclampsia patients where most extant single-cell atlases focus on term versus preterm placenta, or largely examine trophoblast biology with a much rarer subset of immune cells. While the authors present vast amounts of data at both the protein and RNA transcript level, we, the reviewers, feel this manuscript is still in need of much more clarity in its main messaging, and more discretion in including only key data that supports this main message most effectively.

Strengths:

(1) This study combines human and mouse analyses and allows for some amount of mechanistic insight into the role of pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory macrophages in the pathogenesis of pre-eclampsia (PE), and their interaction with Th17 cells.

(2) Importantly, they do this using matched cohorts across normal pregnancy and common PE comorbidities like gestation diabetes (GDM).

(3) The authors have developed clear translational opportunities from these "big data" studies by moving to pursue potential IGF1-based interventions.

results.result: The manuscript provides background information on preeclampsia (PE) and gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), stating that PE is a major cause of maternal mortality with heterogeneous causes, is usually complicated by GDM, has a global prevalence of 7-10%, and that delivery is the only specific treatment. GDM is characterized by insulin resistance and is an independent risk factor for PE.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C18-C22 present established medical knowledge about PE and GDM that is well-supported by the cited literature (Chappell et al., 2021; Burton et al., 2019; Grotegut, 2016; Corrêa-Silva et al., 2018; McElwain et al., 2021; McIntyre et al., 2019; Nerenberg et al., 2013; Ostlund et al., 2004; Schneider et al., 2012). However, claim C2 stating PE is "usually" complicated by GDM is potentially misleading as it overstates the frequency of this complication without providing specific prevalence data.

results.result: The manuscript reviews prior literature on immune alterations in PE, including increased pro-inflammatory M1-like macrophages, granulocytes, NK cells, B1 lymphocytes, and γδ T cells, along with decreased anti-inflammatory M2-like macrophages and NKp46+ NK cells. It also discusses the role of adaptive immunity, with CD4+ T cells preferentially differentiating into Th1/Th17 rather than Th2/Treg in PE.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C37 summarize established findings from the literature with appropriate citations (Faas et al., 2014; Yao et al., 2019; Lampé et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2021; Bachmayer et al., 2006; Travis et al., 2020; Jensen et al., 2012; LaMarca et al., 2011; Zhong et al., 2007; Chatterjee et al., 2017; Fukui et al., 2011; Deer et al., 2023; Eghbal-Fard et al., 2019; Fu et al., 2014; Lang et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2020; Saito et al., 2007; Care et al., 2018; Cornelius et al., 2015a; Santner-Nanan et al., 2009; Sasaki et al., 2007; Aneman et al., 2020; Cornelius et al., 2015b; Fu et al., 2013). These claims accurately represent prior work and provide appropriate context for the current study.

results.result: CyTOF analysis revealed PE-specific immune alterations in placental tissue: increased frequencies of memory-like Th17 cells (CD45RA−CCR7+IL-17A+CD4+), memory-like CD8+ T cells (CD38+CXCR3−CCR7+Helios−CD127−CD8+), and pro-inflammatory macrophages (CD206−CD163−CD38midCD107alowCD86midHLA-DRmidCD14+), along with decreased frequencies of anti-inflammatory macrophages (CD206+CD163−CD86midCD33+HLA-DR+CD14+) and gMDSCs (CD11b+CD15hiHLA-DRlow) in PE compared to normal pregnancy (NP). These changes were not observed in GDM or GDM&PE groups, and there were no significant differences in large immune cell subpopulations between groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C8 and C38 are supported by CyTOF data presented in Figures 1-3 and Tables 1-4. The study used appropriate sample sizes (n=9 NP, n=8 PE, n=8 GDM, n=7 GDM&PE) and statistical methods (Kruskal-Wallis test). The PE-specific immune signature is a major finding, though the manuscript acknowledges limitations including differences in BMI and gestational age between groups, and limited GDM&PE samples. The claim that changes were "not found" in GDM/GDM&PE should be interpreted as "not statistically significant" rather than complete absence.

results.result: Memory-like CD4+ T cells in PE placentas showed higher IL-17A and lower Foxp3 expression, were located in placental sinusoids suggesting recent recruitment, and expressed lower levels of immune checkpoint molecules (Tim-3, PD-1) indicating reduced immunosuppressive capacity. Memory-like CD8+ T cells in PE expressed lower PD-1 and TIGIT, suggesting activated cytotoxicity. A specific γδT cell cluster (cluster 15) with lower Tim3 expression was decreased in PE.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C49 are supported by flow cytometry (Figure 2C), immunofluorescence (Figure 2D), and CyTOF data (Figures 2E, 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E-F). The inference about recent recruitment (C43) based on sinusoidal location is reasonable but speculative. The interpretation of lower checkpoint molecule expression as indicating lower immunosuppressive capacity (C46) and activated cytotoxicity (C48) is supported by cited literature (Chen et al., 2022b; Fanelli et al., 2021; Rasmussen et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2016; Morita et al., 2020), though functional assays would strengthen these claims.

results.result: CyTOF analysis of CD11b+ cells revealed decreased frequencies of gMDSCs (CD68midCD39midHLA-DRlowCD11b+CD15+, cluster 12) and anti-inflammatory macrophages (CD206+CD163−CD86midCD33+HLA-DR+, cluster 25), and increased frequencies of pro-inflammatory macrophages (CD206−CD163−CD38midCD107alowCD86midHLA-DRmidCD14+, cluster 23) in PE placentas. These changes were not significant in GDM or GDM&PE groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C53 are supported by CyTOF data shown in Figure 3C and Table 4. The identification of specific macrophage and gMDSC populations using multi-parameter phenotyping is rigorous. The PE-specific nature of these changes (not observed in GDM/GDM&PE) strengthens the finding. Statistical analysis using Kruskal-Wallis test is appropriate for the non-normal distribution confirmed by Shapiro-Wilk test.

results.result: Pearson correlation analysis revealed that pro-inflammatory macrophages were positively correlated with memory-like Th17 cells and memory-like CD8+ T cells, and showed a negative (but not statistically significant) correlation with gMDSCs. Conversely, anti-inflammatory macrophages were positively correlated with gMDSCs and negatively correlated with CD8+ memory-like T cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C11 and C54-C58 are supported by Pearson correlation analysis of CyTOF data shown in Figures 3D-E. The correlations suggest coordinated immune network changes in PE. However, correlation does not establish causation, and the negative correlation between pro-inflammatory macrophages and gMDSCs was not statistically significant (C56), which appropriately tempers the interpretation. The correlation analysis provides important context for subsequent mechanistic experiments.

results.result: The RUPP mouse model of PE showed increased embryo absorption rate, decreased fetal weight and pup crown-rump length, and increased systolic blood pressure (SBP) and urine albumin creatine ratio (UACR) compared to sham-operated controls, indicating successful establishment of a PE mouse model.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C63 are supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-C. The RUPP model is an established approach for studying PE in mice. The phenotypic changes (hypertension, proteinuria, fetal growth restriction) recapitulate key features of human PE. Sample sizes appear adequate (n=9 per group based on Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), and statistical analysis using Student's t-test is appropriate. This validates the model for subsequent mechanistic studies.

results.result: Adoptive transfer of PE-derived macrophages into normal pregnant mice induced PE-like symptoms including increased embryo resorption rate, decreased fetal top-rump length and weight, and increased SBP and UACR.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C68 are supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D-E. This adoptive transfer experiment provides causal evidence that PE-derived macrophages are sufficient to induce PE-like symptoms. However, the manuscript does not specify whether macrophages were depleted in recipient mice before transfer, which could affect interpretation. The experiment demonstrates the pathogenic potential of PE macrophages but does not distinguish between pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory subsets.

results.result: Using GFP transgenic mice, the study demonstrated that the majority of macrophages in the uterus and placenta are of maternal origin (CD11b+GFP−), while fetal-derived macrophages (CD11b+GFP+) represent only a small fraction of the total macrophage population.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 are supported by flow cytometry data from GFP pregnant mice shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G. This experiment is important for validating that macrophages isolated from uterine tissue are predominantly maternal in origin, justifying the use of uterine tissue for macrophage isolation in subsequent experiments. The experimental design (WT female × GFP male) is appropriate for distinguishing maternal from fetal cells.

results.result: RNA-seq comparison of pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory macrophages from RUPP mice revealed 2123 upregulated and 2699 downregulated genes in pro-inflammatory macrophages. Pro-inflammatory macrophages showed increased expression of genes associated with inflammatory response (Ccl7, Ccl8, Ccl2, IL6), complement activation (C1qa, C1qb), and lipid metabolism (Pltp, Apoe), while showing decreased expression of genes associated with angiogenesis (VEGFα, Macro) and tissue development (TGF-β1, Thbs1, Fn1, Slpi).
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C77 are supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4C-D with n=3 per group. The differential gene expression analysis is appropriately conducted with p<0.05 threshold. The functional interpretation of gene expression changes is supported by cited literature (He et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2021; Desrumaux et al., 2016; Jin et al., 2023; Nugteren and Samsom, 2021; Li et al., 2022a). However, the small sample size (n=3) limits statistical power, and validation of key genes by qPCR or protein analysis would strengthen the findings.

results.result: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) revealed that NF-κB signaling and interspecies interaction between organisms were enriched in pro-inflammatory macrophages, while tissue development and epithelial cell morphogenesis were enriched in anti-inflammatory macrophages.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C81 are supported by GSEA shown in Figure 4E. The enrichment of NF-κB signaling in pro-inflammatory macrophages is consistent with their inflammatory phenotype. However, the biological significance of "interspecies interaction between organisms" enrichment is unclear and not discussed. The enrichment of tissue development and epithelial cell morphogenesis in anti-inflammatory macrophages aligns with their proposed role in tissue homeostasis and repair.

results.result: Adoptive transfer of sorted pro-inflammatory macrophages (CD45+F4/80+CD206−) into PLX3397-treated pregnant mice induced PE-like symptoms (increased embryo resorption, decreased fetal parameters, increased SBP and UACR) and altered immune cell frequencies (increased memory-like Th17 and CD8+ T cells, decreased gMDSCs), validating CyTOF findings.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C89 are supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4F-H. This is a critical experiment demonstrating that pro-inflammatory macrophages are sufficient to induce PE-like symptoms and the associated immune changes. The use of PLX3397 to deplete endogenous macrophages is appropriate, though the manuscript notes this drug can cross the placental barrier and potentially affect fetal macrophages. The experiment was replicated using clodronate liposomes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B-E) with similar results, strengthening the conclusions. Sample sizes appear adequate (n=8 per group).

results.result: Single-cell RNA-seq of macrophages from mice injected with pro-inflammatory or anti-inflammatory macrophages revealed that cluster 0 (increased in pro-inflammatory macrophage group) was enriched for inflammatory response and antigen presentation genes (CCL5, CCL8, CALR, IRF7, IL10, IFI44, IFI30, OAS3), while cluster 1 (decreased in pro-inflammatory macrophage group) showed elevated expression of genes associated with VEGF production and tissue development (MMP14, Chil3, EGR1, ATF3, VASP).
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C91 and C98-C102 are supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figures 5D-G. The single-cell analysis provides detailed characterization of macrophage heterogeneity and confirms the distinct phenotypes of pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory macrophages. The GO enrichment analysis appropriately identifies functional differences between clusters. However, the manuscript does not clearly specify the number of cells analyzed or provide quality control metrics for the scRNA-seq data, which are important for assessing data quality.

results.result: Single-cell RNA-seq of T/NK cells revealed that cluster 0, identified as memory-like Th17 cells based on expression of both Th17-associated genes (IL-17a, IL17f, Rora, Il1r1, TNF) and memory markers (Cxcr6, S100a4, CD44), was increased in mice injected with pro-inflammatory macrophages, while clusters 1 and 2 (immunoregulatory T cells) were decreased.
results.evaluation: Claims C12 and C103-C107 are supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figures 6A-C. The identification of memory-like Th17 cells based on co-expression of Th17 and memory markers is well-supported by the data and cited literature (Hang et al., 2019; Leite et al., 2023; Evrard et al., 2023; Bieberich et al., 2021). This finding provides molecular characterization of the memory-like Th17 cells identified by CyTOF in human samples. The inference that cluster 0 represents memory-like Th17 cells (C107) is reasonable based on the gene expression profile.

results.result: ScRNA-seq revealed that clusters 1 and 2 were T cells with immunomodulatory function based on expression of immunoregulation genes (Lef1, Tcf7, Ccr7) and immunomodulation genes (Gata3, GITR, CD28). Cluster 0 (memory-like Th17 cells) in the pro-inflammatory macrophage group showed enrichment for 'positive regulation of response to external stimulus' and 'tumor necrosis factor production' with high expression of TNFSF11, TNF, IL27RA, IGF1R, CD226, and LAMP1, while the control group showed elevated expression of ASS1, EIF5, S100A9, CTLA4, S100A8, and CXCR4 enriched in 'regulation of programmed cell death' and 'cellular biosynthetic process'.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C114 are supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figures 6D-E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B with appropriate citations (Qiu and Du, 2022; Sekine et al., 2020; Esensten et al., 2016; Pai et al., 2023). The GO enrichment analysis provides functional context for the gene expression differences. The identification of IGF1R as highly expressed in memory-like Th17 cells from the pro-inflammatory macrophage group is important for the subsequent mechanistic studies on IGF1-IGF1R signaling.

results.result: CD4+CD44+ T cells from RUPP mice, characterized by increased Th17 and decreased Treg frequencies, induced PE-like symptoms (increased embryo absorption, decreased fetal parameters, increased SBP and UACR) when adoptively transferred into normal pregnant mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C120 are supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 6F) and experimental outcomes (Figures 6G-H). This adoptive transfer experiment provides causal evidence that memory-like T cells from PE mice are sufficient to induce PE-like symptoms. The characterization of transferred cells showing increased Th17/decreased Treg ratio is important for understanding the pathogenic mechanism. Sample sizes appear adequate (n=6 per group). This experiment complements the macrophage transfer studies and supports the proposed immune network model.

results.result: Mice with a history of PE in their first pregnancy showed increased embryo resorption, decreased fetal parameters, increased SBP and UACR, and higher IL-17A levels in memory-like CD4+ T cells during their second pregnancy compared to mice with a history of normal pregnancy, suggesting that memory-like Th17 cells contribute to PE recurrence.
results.evaluation: Claims C14 and C121-C127 are supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-E. This experiment provides evidence for the role of memory-like Th17 cells in PE recurrence, which is clinically relevant given the increased risk of PE in subsequent pregnancies. The citation to Rowe et al., 2012 (C121) appropriately contextualizes the finding within the literature on memory T cells in pregnancy. However, the mechanism by which memory-like Th17 cells persist between pregnancies and contribute to recurrence requires further investigation.

results.result: ScRNA-seq analysis of granulocytes revealed that cluster 3, expressing gMDSC-associated genes (Ly6g, S100a8, Retnlg, Wfdc21), was decreased in the pro-inflammatory macrophage group and showed enrichment for 'tumor necrosis factor production' and 'leukocyte mediated immunity' with high expression of IRF7, EGR1, C1QA, C1QB, CCL2, CSF3R, and TNFRSF1B. Additionally, immunofluorescence revealed increased CD15+CD66b+ neutrophils in PE patient placentas.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C16 and C128-C131 are supported by scRNA-seq data (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A-E) and immunofluorescence (Figure 6—figure supplement 2F). The identification of gMDSCs based on expression of characteristic genes is supported by cited literature (von Wulffen et al., 2023; Kao et al., 2023). The finding of increased neutrophils in PE placentas (C131) is supported by immunofluorescence data and citation to Akkari et al., 2024. However, the functional relationship between gMDSCs and neutrophils is not clearly established, and the GO enrichment results for cluster 3 seem contradictory (decreased frequency but enriched for inflammatory pathways).

results.result: CellPhoneDB analysis revealed increased communication between macrophages and T/NK cells in mice injected with pro-inflammatory macrophages, with significant enhancement of the IGF1-IGF1R ligand-receptor pair. Flow cytometry confirmed increased frequencies of IGF1+CD14+ macrophages and IGF1R+CD4+ T cells in PE placentas. Literature supports that IGF1R signaling promotes Th17 differentiation over Treg differentiation through increased aerobic glycolysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C13 and C132-C138 are supported by CellPhoneDB analysis (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-B), flow cytometry data (Figure 7B), and cited literature (Bekkering et al., 2018; DiToro et al., 2020). The identification of IGF1-IGF1R as a key signaling axis is a major mechanistic finding. However, the sample size for human placenta analysis is small (n=12 NP, n=4 PE), which limits statistical power. The CellPhoneDB analysis provides computational prediction of cell-cell interactions, but experimental validation is needed.

results.result: In vitro co-culture experiments showed that PE-EV-treated macrophages induced higher frequencies of memory-like CD45RO+CCR7+IL-17A+CD4+ cells compared to NP-EV-treated macrophages, and this induction was significantly reduced by treatment with the IGF1R inhibitor BMS-754807.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C141 are supported by in vitro co-culture experiments shown in Figure 7C-D. The use of trophoblast-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) to induce macrophage polarization is based on prior work (Liu et al., 2022, C139). The experiment demonstrates that IGF1R signaling is necessary for pro-inflammatory macrophage-induced memory-like Th17 cell differentiation. Sample size is adequate (n=10 per group). However, the manuscript does not provide details on EV characterization or the concentration of BMS-754807 used, which are important for reproducibility.

results.result: In an LPS-induced PE mouse model with CD4+ T cell depletion and reconstitution, mice injected with CD4+ T cells pre-treated with IGF1R inhibitor BMS-754807 showed decreased embryo resorption, increased fetal parameters, decreased SBP and UACR, and decreased frequency of memory-like Th17 cells at the maternal-fetal interface compared to mice receiving untreated CD4+ T cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C147 are supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7E-H. This in vivo experiment provides causal evidence that IGF1R signaling in CD4+ T cells is necessary for memory-like Th17 cell induction and PE development. The experimental design using anti-CD4 antibody depletion followed by reconstitution with treated or untreated T cells is appropriate. Sample sizes appear adequate (n=6-7 per group). However, the use of LPS to induce PE is a different model than RUPP, which may limit direct comparison. The manuscript does not specify the dose or duration of BMS-754807 treatment.

results.result: The study concludes that pro-inflammatory macrophages orchestrate a PE-specific immune cell network at the maternal-fetal interface, inducing memory-like Th17 cells via IGF1-IGF1R signaling and suppressing gMDSCs, leading to PE-like symptoms and contributing to disease recurrence.
results.evaluation: Claims C17 and C148 represent the overall conclusions of the study, which are supported by the collective evidence from CyTOF, scRNA-seq, and multiple in vivo experiments. The study provides a comprehensive characterization of the PE-specific immune microenvironment and establishes a mechanistic link between pro-inflammatory macrophages, memory-like Th17 cells, and PE pathogenesis through IGF1-IGF1R signaling. However, several limitations should be noted: (1) differences in BMI and gestational age between groups in human samples, (2) limited GDM&PE samples, (3) use of different PE mouse models (RUPP and LPS), (4) potential effects of PLX3397 on fetal macrophages, and (5) lack of functional validation of memory-like Th17 cells in human samples.

results.result: Using CyTOF, the authors identified PE-specific changes in placental immune cell frequencies: increased memory-like Th17 cells, memory-like CD8+ T cells, and pro-inflammatory macrophages, alongside decreased anti-inflammatory macrophages and gMDSCs in PE compared to normal pregnancy, but not in GDM or GDM&PE placentas.
results.evaluation: All reviewers acknowledged these findings as convincing. Reviewer 1 stated the study 'found that placentas from PE cases showed increased frequencies of memory-like Th17 cells, memory-like CD8⁺ T cells, and pro-inflammatory macrophages, alongside decreased levels of anti-inflammatory macrophages and granulocyte myeloid-derived suppressor cells (gMDSCs).' Reviewer 2 noted the authors 'find an increase in macrophages and Th17 cells in patients with pre-eclampsia.' The editor described this as 'convincing evidence.'

results.result: Correlation analysis revealed that pro-inflammatory macrophages were positively correlated with memory-like Th17 and CD8+ T cells, and negatively correlated with gMDSCs, while anti-inflammatory macrophages showed the opposite pattern.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly stated 'Further analysis revealed a positive correlation between pro-inflammatory macrophages and the expanded T cell populations, and a negative correlation with gMDSCs.' No concerns were raised about these correlation findings by any reviewer.

results.result: Adoptive transfer of F4/80+CD206− pro-inflammatory macrophages from PE mice to normal pregnant mice induced memory-like Th17 cells via IGF1-IGF1R signaling, promoted memory-like CD8+ T cells, inhibited gMDSCs, and led to PE-like symptoms including increased blood pressure and embryo resorption.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 described this as a key mechanistic finding: 'transferring a specific subset of pro-inflammatory macrophages...induced the formation of pathogenic memory-like Th17 cells via the IGF1-IGF1R pathway. This cellular interplay not only contributed to the development but also to the recurrence of PE.' Reviewer 2 noted the authors 'demonstrate the putative role of the IGF1-IGF1R axis as the key pathway by which inflammatory macrophages in the placenta skew CD4+ T cells towards an inflammatory IL-17A-secreting phenotype.' The editor confirmed 'convincing evidence.'

results.result: The IGF1-IGF1R ligand-receptor pair was significantly enhanced between macrophages and T cells in PE, and IGF1R inhibition reduced memory-like Th17 cell formation in vitro.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly stated the authors 'demonstrate the putative role of the IGF1-IGF1R axis as the key pathway' and noted this provides 'potential translational opportunities to pursue this pathway in this indication.' Reviewer 1 confirmed the mechanistic insights via 'Single-cell RNA sequencing.' No concerns were raised about the IGF1R inhibitor experiments.

results.result: In vivo IGF1R inhibition (BMS-754807) in CD4+ T cells reduced embryo resorption, improved fetal parameters, decreased blood pressure and proteinuria, and reduced memory-like Th17 cells at the maternal-fetal interface.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 noted the authors 'demonstrate the putative role of the IGF1-IGF1R axis' and emphasized 'potential translational opportunities to pursue this pathway.' Reviewer 1 stated 'Demonstration of the adverse effects of pro-inflammatory macrophages and T cells on pregnancy outcomes through in vivo manipulations' as a strength. No concerns were raised about these therapeutic intervention experiments.

results.result: Memory-like CD4+CD44+ T cells from PE mice induced PE-like symptoms when transferred to normal pregnant mice, and mice with a history of PE showed recurrent PE symptoms in subsequent pregnancies with elevated memory-like Th17 cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly noted the findings showed 'This cellular interplay not only contributed to the development but also to the recurrence of PE.' Reviewer 1 also listed as a strength 'Demonstration of the adverse effects of pro-inflammatory macrophages and T cells on pregnancy outcomes through in vivo manipulations.' No concerns were raised about the recurrence experiments.

results.result: Bulk RNA-seq revealed that pro-inflammatory macrophages showed increased expression of inflammatory response genes (Ccl7, Ccl8, IL6), complement activation genes (C1qa, C1qb), and lipid metabolism genes, while showing decreased expression of angiogenesis and tissue development genes. Pro-inflammatory macrophages were enriched for NF-κB signaling while anti-inflammatory macrophages were enriched for tissue development pathways.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 noted as a strength 'Incorporation of cutting-edge and complementary techniques such as CyTOF, scRNA-seq, bulk RNA-seq, and flow cytometry.' No specific concerns were raised about the bulk RNA-seq characterization of macrophage phenotypes. The transcriptional profiling supports the functional classification of macrophage subsets.

results.result: Single-cell RNA-seq of macrophages revealed that pro-inflammatory macrophage injection increased cluster 0 (expressing inflammatory response and antigen presentation genes) and decreased cluster 1 (expressing tissue development genes). scRNA-seq of T cells showed increased cluster 0 (memory-like Th17 cells expressing IL-17a, Rora, and memory markers Cxcr6, S100a4, CD44) and decreased immunomodulatory clusters 1 and 2.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 stated 'Single-cell RNA sequencing provided mechanistic insights' and listed as a strength 'Incorporation of cutting-edge and complementary techniques such as CyTOF, scRNA-seq, bulk RNA-seq, and flow cytometry.' Reviewer 1 also noted 'Identification of specific immune cell populations and their roles in PE' as a strength. No concerns were raised about the scRNA-seq cluster identification or characterization.

results.result: Memory-like CD45RO+CCR7+CD4+ T cells in PE placentas showed higher IL-17A and lower Foxp3 expression, were located in placental sinusoids, and expressed lower levels of immune checkpoint molecules (Tim-3, PD-1) in CD4+ memory T cells and (PD-1, TIGIT) in CD8+ memory T cells.
results.evaluation: These findings are part of the comprehensive characterization of PE-specific immune changes that reviewers found convincing. Reviewer 1 noted 'Identification of specific immune cell populations and their roles in PE' as a strength. The immunofluorescence and flow cytometry validation of CyTOF findings were not questioned by reviewers.

results.result: The RUPP mouse model and adoptive transfer of PE-derived macrophages both successfully induced PE-like symptoms including increased embryo resorption, decreased fetal parameters, elevated blood pressure, and increased proteinuria.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 stated as a strength 'Utilization of both human placental samples and multiple mouse models to explore the mechanisms linking inflammatory macrophages and T cells to preeclampsia (PE).' The establishment of the PE mouse model was not questioned by any reviewer and serves as the foundation for subsequent mechanistic experiments.

results.result: The majority of macrophages in the uterus and placenta are of maternal origin (CD11b+GFP−), with fetal-derived macrophages representing only a small fraction.
results.evaluation: This finding was not questioned by reviewers and provides important context for the macrophage transfer experiments. It clarifies that the transferred maternal macrophages are the relevant population in PE pathogenesis.

results.result: Adoptive transfer of sorted pro-inflammatory macrophages (but not anti-inflammatory macrophages) to normal pregnant mice induced PE-like symptoms and increased memory-like Th17 and CD8+ T cells while decreasing gMDSCs, validating the CyTOF findings.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly stated as a strength 'Demonstration of the adverse effects of pro-inflammatory macrophages and T cells on pregnancy outcomes through in vivo manipulations.' This experiment directly validates the causal role of pro-inflammatory macrophages and was not questioned by reviewers.

results.result: scRNA-seq identified gMDSCs (cluster 3) expressing Ly6g, S100a8, Retnlg, and Wfdc21, which were enriched for inflammatory response genes in the pro-inflammatory macrophage group. Immunofluorescence revealed increased CD15+CD66b+ neutrophils in PE patients.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 noted 'Identification of specific immune cell populations and their roles in PE' as a strength. The characterization of gMDSCs and neutrophils complements the main findings about macrophages and T cells. No concerns were raised about these supporting findings.

results.result: CellPhoneDB analysis showed increased communication counts and signaling pathway numbers between macrophages and T/NK cells in mice injected with pro-inflammatory macrophages.
results.evaluation: This computational analysis supports the mechanistic findings about macrophage-T cell interactions. Reviewer 2 noted the study 'allows for some amount of mechanistic insight into the role of pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory macrophages in the pathogenesis of pre-eclampsia (PE), and their interaction with Th17 cells.' No concerns were raised about the cell-cell communication analysis.

results.result: Preeclampsia is usually complicated by gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM).
results.evaluation: While this claim is presented as background knowledge, the study design includes GDM and GDM&PE groups specifically because of this relationship. However, the word 'usually' may overstate the frequency of this complication. Reviewer 2 noted as a strength that the authors 'do this using matched cohorts across normal pregnancy and common PE comorbidities like gestation diabetes (GDM),' acknowledging GDM as a 'common' rather than 'usual' comorbidity.

results.result: There were no significant differences in the proportion of large immune cell subpopulations (T cells, macrophages, granulocytes, etc.) comparing PE, GDM, and GDM&PE groups to the normal pregnancy group.
results.evaluation: This finding establishes that the PE-specific changes occur at the level of immune cell subsets rather than major populations. Reviewer 1 noted 'Identification of specific immune cell populations and their roles in PE' as a strength, implying acceptance of the subset-level rather than population-level changes. No concerns were raised about this finding.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate claims C3-C8 about PE-specific immune signatures (increased memory-like Th17 cells, memory-like CD8+ T cells, pro-inflammatory macrophages; decreased anti-inflammatory macrophages and gMDSCs). Both find these claims SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes methodological details (CyTOF, sample sizes, statistical methods) and limitations (BMI/gestational age differences, limited GDM&PE samples). Peer reviewers describe findings as 'convincing evidence.' OpenEval also addresses C38 (subset-level changes) which peer reviewers cover separately in R16.

Perfect match on claims C9-C11, C54-C58 regarding correlations between pro-inflammatory macrophages and expanded T cell populations, and negative correlation with gMDSCs. Both find these correlation analyses SUPPORTED. OpenEval appropriately notes that correlation does not establish causation and that the negative correlation with gMDSCs was not statistically significant. Peer Reviewer 1 explicitly acknowledged these correlation findings without concerns.

Both address the overall mechanistic model (C13, C17) involving pro-inflammatory macrophages inducing memory-like Th17 cells via IGF1-IGF1R pathway contributing to PE development and recurrence. OpenEval R19 focuses on IGF1-IGF1R signaling and cell-cell communication (C13, C132-C138), while OpenEval R22 addresses the overall conclusions (C17, C148). Peer R3 encompasses the broader mechanistic findings (C12-C17). Both find SUPPORTED with peer reviewers noting 'convincing evidence' and 'potential translational opportunities.'

Both evaluate IGF1-IGF1R pathway experiments. OpenEval R20 addresses in vitro co-culture experiments (C139-C141) showing IGF1R signaling is necessary for pro-inflammatory macrophage-induced memory-like Th17 differentiation. Peer R4 covers broader IGF1-IGF1R axis findings (C134, C137-C138, C140-C141). Both find SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers emphasize translational potential. OpenEval notes missing details on EV characterization and BMS-754807 concentration.

Perfect match on claims C142-C147 regarding in vivo experiments showing IGF1R signaling in CD4+ T cells is necessary for memory-like Th17 cell induction and PE development. Both find SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers note 'potential translational opportunities' and 'demonstration of adverse effects through in vivo manipulations.' OpenEval notes the use of different PE model (LPS vs RUPP) and missing details on BMS-754807 dosing.

Both address adoptive transfer experiments showing memory-like T cells from PE mice induce PE-like symptoms (C116-C120) and PE recurrence experiments (C122-C127). OpenEval separates these into R16 (development) and R17 (recurrence), while peer R6 covers both aspects together. Both find SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers note findings contribute to 'development and recurrence of PE' and demonstrate 'adverse effects through in vivo manipulations.'

Both address bulk RNA-seq characterization of macrophage phenotypes (C71-C77) and GSEA results (C78-C81). OpenEval R10 covers RNA-seq differential expression, R11 covers GSEA. Peer R7 addresses both together. Both find SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers note 'incorporation of cutting-edge techniques' as strength. OpenEval notes small sample size (n=3) and suggests validation would strengthen findings.

Both evaluate scRNA-seq findings. OpenEval R13 addresses macrophage heterogeneity (C90-C91, C98-C102), while OpenEval R14 addresses memory-like Th17 cell characterization (C12, C103-C107). Peer R8 covers both aspects together (C90-C91, C98-C107). Both find SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers note 'mechanistic insights' and 'identification of specific immune cell populations' as strengths. OpenEval notes missing quality control metrics for scRNA-seq data.

Both address characterization of memory-like Th17 cells including sinusoidal location, checkpoint molecule expression, and activated cytotoxicity (C39-C47). OpenEval covers C39-C49 with flow cytometry, immunofluorescence, and CyTOF validation. Peer R9 covers C39-C42, C44-C45, C47. Both find SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers note this as part of 'identification of specific immune cell populations.' OpenEval notes some interpretations are speculative and would benefit from functional assays.

Both address establishment of PE mouse models. OpenEval R7 covers RUPP model validation (C59-C63), R8 covers adoptive transfer of PE macrophages (C64-C68). Peer R10 covers both aspects (C59-C68) as part of 'utilization of multiple mouse models.' Both find SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes RUPP model appropriately recapitulates PE features; for adoptive transfer, notes missing details on macrophage depletion in recipients.

Perfect match on claims C69-C70 showing macrophages isolated from uterine tissue are predominantly maternal in origin using GFP pregnant mice. Both find SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers note this provides important context for macrophage transfer experiments without raising concerns. OpenEval notes the experimental design (WT female × GFP male) is appropriate for distinguishing maternal from fetal cells.

Perfect match on claims C82-C89 regarding adoptive transfer of pro-inflammatory macrophages inducing PE-like symptoms and immune changes. Both find SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers explicitly note 'demonstration of adverse effects through in vivo manipulations' as strength. OpenEval notes appropriate use of PLX3397 for macrophage depletion with replication using clodronate liposomes, though mentions potential placental barrier crossing as limitation.

Both address characterization of gMDSCs and neutrophils. OpenEval R18 covers scRNA-seq identification of gMDSCs (C15-C16, C128-C131) and notes contradictory GO enrichment results. Peer R13 covers C128-C131 as supporting findings complementing main macrophage/T cell results. Both find SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers note 'identification of specific immune cell populations' as strength without raising concerns about the contradictory enrichment patterns.

Both address cell-cell communication analysis identifying IGF1-IGF1R signaling. OpenEval R19 covers CellPhoneDB analysis and flow cytometry validation (C13, C132-C138). Peer R14 covers computational analysis (C132-C133) supporting macrophage-T cell interactions. Both find SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers note study 'allows for mechanistic insight.' OpenEval notes small human sample size (n=12 NP, n=4 PE) and that computational predictions need experimental validation.

Both address claim C2 that PE is 'usually' complicated by GDM. OpenEval finds claims C1-C2, C18-C22 SUPPORTED but notes C2 'potentially misleading as it overstates the frequency' without specific prevalence data. Peer reviewer finds UNCERTAIN, noting 'usually' may overstate frequency and that GDM is better described as 'common' rather than 'usual' comorbidity. Both identify the same concern about overstating the relationship.

Both address claim C38 that PE-specific changes occur at subset level rather than major population level. OpenEval R3 includes C38 with main PE immune signature findings (C3-C8, C38) and finds SUPPORTED. Peer R16 addresses C38 separately, also finding SUPPORTED and noting 'identification of specific immune cell populations' as strength. Both agree this establishes the specificity of PE-associated immune changes.

OpenEval R11 addresses GSEA results (C78-C81) showing NF-κB enrichment in pro-inflammatory macrophages and tissue development pathways in anti-inflammatory macrophages. Peer R7 addresses broader transcriptional profiling (C71-C81) including both RNA-seq and GSEA. Both find SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers note 'incorporation of cutting-edge techniques' without specific concerns about GSEA interpretations.

OpenEval R14 addresses scRNA-seq characterization of memory-like Th17 cells (C12, C103-C107). Peer R8 covers broader scRNA-seq findings including both macrophages (C90-C91, C98-C102) and T cells (C103-C107). Both find SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers note 'mechanistic insights' and 'identification of specific immune cell populations.' OpenEval provides detailed molecular characterization based on co-expression of Th17 and memory markers.

OpenEval R15 addresses scRNA-seq analysis of memory-like Th17 cells showing differential gene expression and IGF1R upregulation (C108-C114). Peer R8 covers broader scRNA-seq characterization (C90-C107) that includes these findings. Both find SUPPORTED. OpenEval specifically notes IGF1R identification as important for subsequent mechanistic studies. Peer reviewers acknowledge mechanistic insights without specific concerns.

OpenEval R17 addresses PE recurrence experiments (C14, C121-C127) showing memory-like Th17 cells contribute to recurrence. Peer R6 covers both development (C116-C120) and recurrence (C122-C127) experiments together. Both find SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers note findings show 'cellular interplay contributed to development and recurrence of PE.' OpenEval notes clinical relevance but indicates mechanism of persistence requires further investigation.

OpenEval R22 presents overall conclusions (C17, C148) synthesizing the complete mechanistic model. Peer R3 addresses the mechanistic findings (C12-C17) including the overall conclusion C17. Both find SUPPORTED with 'convincing evidence.' OpenEval provides comprehensive summary of limitations (BMI/gestational age differences, limited GDM&PE samples, different PE models, PLX3397 effects, lack of functional validation in human samples). Peer reviewers focus on translational potential.

OpenEval R1 addresses background claims about PE and GDM (C1-C2, C18-C22) from introduction, finding them SUPPORTED but noting C2 overstates frequency. Only C2 has corresponding peer evaluation (R15). Other background claims (C1, C18-C22) establishing medical knowledge about PE and GDM have no specific peer review evaluation.

OpenEval R2 addresses extensive background literature review claims (C23-C37) about immune dysregulation in PE and GDM, finding them SUPPORTED as accurate representation of prior work. No corresponding peer review evaluation found - peer reviewers did not separately evaluate these literature summary claims.

OpenEval R5 addresses identification of specific macrophage and gMDSC populations by CyTOF (C50-C53), finding SUPPORTED with rigorous multi-parameter phenotyping. No corresponding peer review evaluation found - these specific population identification claims were not separately evaluated by peer reviewers, though related findings appear in other peer evaluations.

OpenEval R8 addresses adoptive transfer of PE-derived macrophages inducing PE-like symptoms (C64-C68), finding SUPPORTED as causal evidence. While peer R10 covers related model establishment claims (C59-C68), the specific adoptive transfer experiment (C64-C68) is not separately distinguished in peer reviews from RUPP model validation (C59-C63).
